content.thinking:
I'm working out the bird's local coordinate frame, defining facing and left vectors so the geometry orients correctly relative to its direction of travel.

With that resolved, I'm planning the ellipsoid parts for bird anatomy using scaled, aimed shapes along the local axes, and checking which parameters (dir, axis, scale) the part builder supports. I also need to sample the head's surface for the crown position using a raycast against the lofted mesh, then set up the joint hierarchy for the bird body parented appropriately.

Still placing bird parts...

I'm working out the lower beak dimensions and how to pose the jaw open at an 18° angle, figuring out which rotation axis actually tips the beak downward given the bird's yaw rotation - testing the cross product of the local X axis with the forward direction to confirm it points down.

Next I'm placing the eyes as small spheres embedded in the head sphere surface, offset toward the front, with a black pupil sphere and a tiny white highlight sphere layered on top; I'm skipping the cheek blush detail for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the bird's color scheme as a paint function based on surface normal and body-relative position—blue on the crown transitioning to a lighter orange near the chin and throat using a countershading approach, with the body split by normal direction into blue upper regions and orange-tinted lower/front regions.

Shaping the wing outline...

Still shaping the tail feathers...

I'll keep the thickness axis simple and horizontal to avoid shearing, and instead lift the tail by posing the tail joint itself—rotating the backward-pointing bone upward with a positive lateral-axis angle.

Now I'm adding a bird tail with feathers extruded from that bone, plus a small crest of spikes leaning back on top of the head. For the capybara's sleepy eye, I'm sketching an SVG decal with a dark ellipse base, white highlight circles, and a curved eyelid shape covering the top.

Since the flat lid color didn't work against mottled fur, I'm switching to drawing the eye as a half-moon dome shape with a flat curved top, filled dark, with a thicker stroked lid line and a little lash flick at the outer corner, plus the highlight circles layered inside.

Scaling stroke widths proportionally for the larger 128px output, I'm placing the lash flick on the correct side depending on mirroring. For the blush decal I'm building a small ellipse in a pinkish-orange tone sized to sit on the cheek, with a few short darker hatch strokes for texture, then moving on to sketch the ear shape as a rounded flap on top of the head.

Drafting ear geometry...

Working out the mirrored rotation for the right ear so both tilt outward symmetrically, keeping thickness along z so the plate faces forward. Then I'll add a smaller pink inner-ear shape, slightly offset forward of the main ear plate to simulate depth.

Now defining the paint function for the ear's inner pink region using an ellipse test on the outline coordinates combined with the forward-facing normal, falling back to dark fur elsewhere. I'm setting up the ear joints with hinges at the base, aimed upward, and deciding to skip extra fur rim cards on the ears for simplicity.

Moving to the lower jaw, I'm sketching a loft along several z-stations with specified widths and heights to shape the jawbone, checking how it aligns against the underside of the upper head.

I'm checking that the jaw fits snugly inside the head geometry, then adding a lighter chin tone and round cheek/jowl spheres near the sides of the face for a chubby capybara look, adjusting the head loft width where needed. I confirm the head and body silhouettes line up reasonably well in height, decide to skip eyebrows, and move on to work on the hindquarters next.

Now I'm defining the leg-building function, computing joint positions for the front leg (shoulder down to foot) using mirrored X coordinates for left/right sides, with two bent segments to create a visible elbow joint, and naming each joint point accordingly.

For the hind leg, I'm setting hip and foot target positions with three segment lengths that sum longer than the direct distance, forcing a bent knee-forward, hock-back configuration so the final segment stays roughly vertical, and labeling the joints hip, knee, hock, and ankle.

For the front leg, I'm working through the naming convention—three points means two spans plus a tip, so shoulder and elbow mark the joints while wrist labels the tip endpoint.

Now I'm sweeping each leg chain with a radius profile that tapers from thick at the hip/shoulder down to thin at the foot, defining a set of radius values along the limb for front and hind legs separately, checking that the hip radius stays reasonable relative to half the body width. For the foot, I'm placing a paw pad as a flattened, slightly elongated sphere positioned just above ground level and offset forward, colored a dark brown.

Now I'm adding toes: four small capsule shapes per front foot spread outward with slight spacing, angled forward and down from the toe joint to a tip near the ground, each capped with a small dark nail cone at the end, and fanning the toe offsets outward using a scaled spread factor per toe index.

I'm tallying up the joint hierarchy—spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, tail, legs with their toe segments, plus a separate bird skeleton with body, head, beak, wings, and tail—landing around 45 joints total, which feels workable. Now I'm setting up a helper function to build ellipsoid body parts tied to bones at given positions with custom radii and colors.

I'm designing fur tufts for the body using a small SVG texture with pointed stroke shapes—a central tuft plus flank variants—tinted by a coat color read from the root, then applying those as card-based fur geometry sized and leaned across the body frames.

I'm scattering tuft cards across the body surface while filtering out the head area to keep a shaggy belly look, but noticing that the default card orientation would face edge-on from the side, so I'm adjusting the lean angle to tip them along the surface flow instead.

On the flanks, since the normal points sideways, the flattened flow runs back and down, making the card's width run vertically so it reads face-on from the side -- good for visibility. I'll use `cross: true` on the tufts so they're readable from multiple angles rather than just front/back.

Skipping eyebrows and lashes, chest/chin tufts can ride along with the general scatter. For whiskers, I'm setting up curved strands rigged to the head bone, starting near the muzzle and bowing outward with slight vertical offsets per strand, using thin rigid caps and a dark brown color, though a cream tone might read better for visibility against the fur.

Now I'm sketching the mouth line as a sweep, planning to check it visually once rendered. For the flower behind the left ear, I'm positioning a yellow center sphere at the ear base and arranging white petals in a ring around it using looped angle calculations to place each petal in the forward-facing plane.

Working out petal rotations and flower placement near the ear base...

I'll cast a ray down to find the hit point on the head surface, then build a local frame from the normal to orient the flower petals flat against the surface, scaling them thin and angling them outward from a center point. Both the bird crest and flower placements look fine, so I'll preview and adjust from there.

Now I'm setting up the bird's local coordinate frame using up, forward, and left vectors derived from the crown position, so I can place parts relative to the crown hit point.

I'm defining the body loft with its bone chain (hips, spine, neck), the head loft rigged to the head joint, and the jaw loft on the jaw bone. Then I'm working out the eye decal placement by finding the nearest surface point on the head near the target coordinates, using the hit normal for orientation and a small size.

Writing fur paint code...

Still defining the skeleton structure...

Still defining joints and parts...

I'm sketching the ear outline shape with rounded tips, and now working out the nose bump as a small dark oval sitting on the bridge of the head.

For the nose pad placement, I'm uncertain how far the loft's rounded end cap extends the head's front boundary, so I'll just build the file and use a box measurement to check the actual geometry before fine-tuning eye placement.
